profiles.meeting_scenario: A mid-sized international trade law firm's arbitration and commercial contracts team is holding a troubleshooting meeting after a client alert draft on CISG Article 11 and the Model Law writing requirement came back with conflicting partner comments. The draft argues that the CISG's acceptance of non-written international sales contracts may justify a more arbitration-friendly approach when assessing whether the parties formed an arbitration agreement tied to that sales relationship. One partner said the piece overstates enforceability risk, while another said it understates the possibility of a doctrinal shift. The two participants must diagnose why the draft is drawing opposite reactions, identify the real source of doctrinal confusion, and decide how to revise the alert so it is internally consistent and safe to publish. The agenda is to pinpoint where the analysis is talking past itself, determine what legal problem actually needs fixing, and agree on a revision plan for the next draft. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for the article: what proposition to narrow, what comparison to keep, and what caveats to add.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Cross-border commercial arbitration, New York Convention enforcement, UNCITRAL Model Law implementation issues
members.background: Elena trained in New York and Singapore, has spent the last eight years handling jurisdictional fights and award-enforcement strategy for trading companies, and regularly edits client-facing thought leadership on arbitration formation and separability.
members.private_state: Elena wants the article to remain bold enough to attract attention from arbitration-focused clients, but she is quietly concerned about creating a statement that litigators on the other side could later quote as the firm's position on informal arbitration consent.
hidden_assumptions: If the article says there is a possible 'shift,' readers will understand that to mean a gradual interpretive movement in court reasoning, not a claim that current black-letter law already accepts oral arbitration agreements in Model Law jurisdictions.

The practical problem is whether tribunals and courts may become less hostile to finding consent when the arbitration clause is embedded in a broader sales relationship governed by instruments like the CISG, rather than whether the formal writing requirement has literally disappeared.

When discussing the 'writing requirement,' sophisticated readers will naturally distinguish Article 7 option-style Model Law formulations and New York Convention compliance issues from domestic contract formation rules, so the article does not need to restate those layers each time.
A fix that makes the alert 'safer' means adding doctrinal caveats and framing limits while preserving the forward-looking thesis.
References to the 'agreement' in this piece will be heard as the arbitration agreement unless explicitly narrowed, because that is the core audience hook.

members.name: Marcus Vale
members.expertise: CISG contract formation, comparative sales law, drafting and litigation support for cross-border supply agreements
members.background: Marcus studied in Germany and England, clerked for a commercial court judge who handled CISG disputes, and now supports the firm's trade practice by translating doctrinal developments into practical client alerts for exporters and distributors.
members.private_state: Marcus wants to prevent the alert from implying more doctrinal convergence than currently exists, because several of his clients rely on strict written arbitration clauses and he does not want the firm's publication to blur the line between sales contract formation and arbitration consent.
hidden_assumptions: If the article invokes CISG Article 11, the central issue is the formation of the sales contract itself, and any mention of arbitration must remain clearly secondary and analytically separate.

The real drafting problem is that the piece seems to treat the absence of a writing requirement for the sales contract as if it could carry over to the arbitration clause, which risks collapsing two distinct consent inquiries.
When lawyers say the alert should be 'tightened,' that ordinarily means trimming claims so they track currently accepted doctrine rather than preserving a provocative thesis with added caveats.

The relevant 'writing requirement' for troubleshooting this draft is the formal validity threshold for the arbitration agreement under applicable arbitration law and enforcement instruments, not a broader evidentiary or commercial practice question.
References to the 'agreement' in this piece will ordinarily be understood as the underlying sales agreement unless the text expressly singles out the arbitration clause.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether 'the agreement' can exist without words in the way the draft currently suggests.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the arbitration agreement, because she is focused on whether adjudicators might infer arbitral consent more flexibly in a CISG-governed transactional setting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means the underlying international sales contract, because for him Article 11 is about the validity of the sales bargain and not the separate arbitration clause.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this doctrinal setting both contracts are discussed in the same paragraph and are closely linked factually, so using the generic phrase 'the agreement' sounds perfectly natural and neither participant feels a need to specify which layer of agreement is in view.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the article needs to be 'safer' before publication.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena thinks 'safer' means preserving the central thesis while adding enough caveat language, jurisdictional qualification, and tone control to avoid overclaiming.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus thinks 'safer' means removing or substantially narrowing the thesis so the article does not invite readers to infer any doctrinal carryover from CISG Article 11 to arbitration agreement formal validity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Editorial meetings routinely use evaluative terms like 'safer,' 'tighter,' and 'more careful' without defining publication thresholds, and both participants sincerely believe they are advocating a standard risk-management edit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer repeatedly to 'the writing requirement' as the doctrinal bottleneck.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking mainly of the Model Law and New York Convention-related formal requirement for the arbitration agreement and how modern practice may interpret compliance flexibly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus is thinking first about the contrast between CISG Article 11's non-formality rule for sales contracts and domestic or arbitral-law formality rules, with emphasis on not conflating them.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the seed issue explicitly juxtaposes CISG Article 11 and the Model Law, both legal formality regimes are on the table from the start, making shorthand reference to 'the writing requirement' feel shared even though each person mentally anchors it to a different legal object.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'reframe around formation'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They converge on a plan to 'reframe the piece around formation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes this means narrowing the discussion to formation of arbitral consent within a commercial relationship already shaped by CISG-friendly norms on informal contracting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes this means refocusing the article on formation of the underlying sales contract and treating arbitration only as a cautionary contrast near the end.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Formation is the obvious umbrella concept connecting both doctrines, so the phrase sounds like a clean compromise; its ambiguity lies in the unnoticed boundary of which formation question is included.

turns.inner_thought: The partner comments are reacting to different levels of boldness. One read the draft as if we were already saying black-letter arbitration law has moved; the other liked the forward signal. I need to keep the thesis alive but make clear that the writing requirement is still a doctrinal bottleneck in the Model Law/New York Convention sense, not something the piece is pretending has vanished.
turns.utterance: We got two completely opposite reactions to the same draft, which usually means the analysis is sliding between ideas without admitting it. I think we need to pinpoint where Article 11 and the writing requirement are rubbing against each other in a way that makes the piece sound broader than it means to.

turns.inner_thought: The clean part is straightforward CISG doctrine: parties can have a sales contract without formal words. The trouble starts when the draft lets that proposition bleed into arbitration consent. If we keep saying the agreement can exist informally without separating the two layers, readers will think we're collapsing them.
turns.utterance: Yes. To me, the draft is strongest when it stays with the basic commercial point that the agreement can exist without formal words in this setting. It gets much weaker once it starts extending that intuition beyond the place where Article 11 is doing real work.

turns.inner_thought: He is right that the agreement point needs tightening, but I still want the article to suggest that tribunals and courts may infer arbitral consent less rigidly when the clause sits inside an informal trading relationship. Safer should mean caveated, not gutted.
turns.utterance: I agree the agreement point needs tightening. But I don't want us to edit out the reason the piece is interesting, which is that decision-makers may become less rigid about consent in this kind of factual setting. If we do it properly, the article can be safer without becoming flat.

turns.inner_thought: Safer means trimming the thesis so no one reads carryover from Article 11 into arbitral formal validity. We need a cleaner wall between sales formation and the writing requirement; otherwise exporters who rely on written clauses will hate this alert.
turns.utterance: Right, but making it safer has to mean we separate Article 11 from the writing requirement more cleanly. At the moment, the draft leaves room for a reader to think one is displacing the other, and I don't think we want that.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with more separation if the shift idea remains. Reframe around formation, but for me that means formation of arbitral consent in a commercial environment shaped by informal contracting norms. And describe the writing requirement as being interpreted with more openness, not abolished.
turns.utterance: I think we can keep the doctrinal-movement idea if we reframe the piece around formation. Then the writing issue reads less like an on-off switch and more like a question of how open modern decision-makers are in assessing what happened between the parties.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Reframe around formation means lead with how the sales contract is concluded in practice, then treat arbitration as a separate and later caution. If we structure it that way, the article stops implying convergence where there really isn't any.
turns.utterance: I think reframing around formation works. If we lead with how these transactions are actually concluded in practice, then bring in arbitration afterward as a distinct formal step, the analysis should feel a lot cleaner.

turns.inner_thought: That structure is useful, as long as we preserve the point that the surrounding relationship can matter when tribunals assess arbitral consent. I need at least one paragraph that keeps the client-facing hook alive.
turns.utterance: That structure sounds right to me. I would just want to preserve a paragraph explaining why the surrounding commercial relationship can still matter when tribunals assess the agreement, so we don't lose the practical payoff.

turns.inner_thought: I can accept that paragraph if it's framed as context rather than doctrinal transfer. The alert must say plainly that the writing requirement still stands and nothing here means automatic enforceability of a clause that was never properly concluded.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable with that, so long as the article is explicit that the writing requirement still stands and that we're not implying automatic enforceability just because the commercial context points in one direction.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. Safer means layering in caveats while keeping the forward-looking point: market practice may influence how arbitral consent is evaluated. I just need to avoid language that opposing counsel could quote as our firm endorsing informal arbitration clauses across the board.
turns.utterance: Exactly. The goal is to make the draft safer while still keeping the forward-looking point that market practice may shape how the agreement is evaluated. If we control the tone, I think both concerns can live in the same piece.

turns.inner_thought: A clean sequence will discipline the whole piece: Article 11 first for the sales contract, then a contrast on the writing requirement, then maybe a very modest closing note that courts are watching commercial reality. That should neutralize the overstatement problem.
turns.utterance: Then maybe the revision sequence is: first clarify what Article 11 is doing, then add a contrast paragraph on the writing requirement, and then close with a modest note on possible doctrinal movement. That would make the progression much easier to follow.

turns.inner_thought: Yes. I can rewrite the opening so it says the piece is about formation and does not sound as if informal contracting automatically equals arbitral consent. But I will still leave room for the thesis that tribunals may infer consent more flexibly in these settings.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll revise the thesis sentence so the piece is framed around formation and doesn't read as if informal contracting automatically establishes consent. That should take some heat out of the opening.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll mark every place where 'the agreement' could confuse the reader and every place where 'the writing requirement' is doing too much work. If those references are cleaned up, the article should track accepted doctrine closely enough to publish.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll go through and mark the sections where the agreement and the writing requirement need cleaner language, and where the piece should be safer in its transitions. Once that's done, the next draft should be publishable.
